A.body:
An office key can open the door. It cannot give you permission to take the equipment.

That distinction matters when approving work, too. A familiar account or company system is only part of the evidence.

Cloudflare reported that account access credentials stolen in the October 2023 Okta compromise were mistakenly considered unused and left unchanged. Attackers later used them to enter its Atlassian work environment.

The digital key still worked. That did not make the person using it entitled to enter.

A separate CERT-In advisory from October 2026 shows the distinction at the payment stage. Attackers used stolen access credentials to send direct computer-to-computer payment requests from the victims’ own recognized company systems. They bypassed application checks and moved funds to accounts controlled by attackers.

The requests came through accepted systems. The payments still lacked permission.

I’d bring that distinction into one practical review: choose a sensitive request you approve and trace what proves this particular action is permitted.

Can you connect it to an approved record covering the action, recipient and amount, where relevant? What stops it proceeding if that evidence is missing?

“Those are our account details” or “it came from our systems” leaves that question unanswered.

The office key is only an illustration. Digital access details can be copied and used remotely; a physical lock cannot capture the checks needed for a payment. These separate reports also do not prove that any particular safeguard would have prevented the incidents.

They do give managers a useful distinction to inspect: evidence that access works, and evidence that the requested action has approval.

#Leadership #RiskManagement #CyberSecurity

B.body:
An office key lets you open the door. It doesn’t give you permission to take the equipment home.

That distinction matters when approving work, too. A familiar account can make a request look legitimate before anyone checks what it is asking to do.

Cloudflare’s February 2024 incident account gives the key part a concrete meaning. It reports that account access details stolen in the October 2023 Okta compromise were mistakenly considered unused and left unchanged. Attackers later used them to enter its Atlassian work systems.

The lock still accepted the key.

A separate CERT-In report from October 2026 shows why permission for the particular action deserves its own check. Attackers used stolen access details to send fund-transfer requests directly between computer systems, from the victims’ own recognized company systems. Those requests bypassed application checks and moved money into accounts used to receive the stolen funds.

Recognized access. Unauthorized payments.

These are different reports about different systems. They illustrate the distinction between accepted access and permitted action; they don’t prove that any particular safeguard would have prevented either incident. And the key is only an illustration: digital access details can be copied and used remotely. No equipment theft is being alleged at Cloudflare.

My practical takeaway is to inspect one sensitive request you’re responsible for approving. Identify the evidence that permits that specific action: the approved record, its scope, the intended recipient and any applicable amount limit.

Then check whether that evidence must actually be verified before the action happens.

A familiar account or company tells you something about where a request appears to come from. Approval needs evidence about what it is allowed to do.

sources.article: CIAD-2026-0046 Threat Actors Exploiting Payment and Disbursement APIs for Unauthorized Fund Transfers in BFSI Entities Original Issue Date: October 09, 2026 Severity Rating: Critical Description CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin has observed multiple cyber attack campaigns targeting non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers and wallet operators. Threat actors compromise internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints, steal payment aggregator/gateway and partner-bank API credentials, and invoke disbursal/fund-transfer APIs directly from within the entities' own whitelisted infrastructure, completely bypassing application-level controls such as loan creation, KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency and per-transaction limits. The fraudulent transactions carry dummy reference identifiers, exceed per-transaction limits, and credit funds to attacker-controlled mule accounts across multiple banks. Analysis of these attacks further indicates the possible use of AI-assisted offensive tooling, with the interval between initial compromise and fraudulent fund transfer reducing significantly in recent incidents. Attacker IPs are predominantly associated with hosting infrastructure. Attack Vector Initial compromise is achieved through: Exploitation of exposed internet-facing applications and application server middleware vulnerabilities. Abuse of deprecated, unauthenticated or unused APIs with unrestricted file-upload functionality. Use of stolen long-lived static API tokens hard-coded in source code. Supply-chain compromise of source-code repositories via forged commits. Exploitation of plaintext credentials in configuration files, source code or databases. Access to applications and remote services lacking MFA. Post-compromise, attackers establish persistence via web shells and backdoors, conduct reconnaissance of payment databases and API integrations, steal payment aggregator/gateway and bank API credentials, and directly invoke disbursal/fund-transfer APIs to execute unauthorized transactions. Key TTPs Observed Direct invocation of disbursal/fund-transfer APIs from whitelisted infrastructure using valid credentials. Bypassing of application-level checks (KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency). Supply of dummy loan/transaction reference numbers with no corresponding records. Rapid execution of multiple high-value transactions through IMPS/NEFT rails. Transfer of funds to mule accounts across multiple banks with immediate withdrawal. Deletion/truncation of logs, tampering with EDR tools, and anti-forensic cleanup. Possible use of AI-assisted offensive frameworks and large numbers of custom scripts. Recommended Actions Enforce MFA for payment platforms, administrative portals, payment/bank APIs and remote access services. Maintain a complete API inventory; formally decommission deprecated and unused APIs. Enforce per-session authentication on all APIs; eliminate long-lived static tokens. Bind multi-stage transaction flows cryptographically so debit-stage APIs cannot be invoked without preceding validation stages. Implement maker-checker or second-level verification for all fund movement. Validate every payout against sanctioned/approved records; reject reference identifiers with no corresponding records. Enforce per-transaction and per-day cumulative ceilings at the API/payment stage. Apply beneficiary validation (penny-drop, name-to-account matching) and velocity limits on all disbursement paths. Restrict outbound (egress) traffic from production servers through allow-listing. Store all API keys and credentials in secure secret management solutions or HSMs; enforce rotation. Implement real-time monitoring of fund transfers with velocity, amount-band and new-beneficiary checks, with automated blocking or holding. Enable near-real-time reconciliation of system records with bank/aggregator statements. Maintain centralized logging and log retention of at least 180 days. Deploy EDR with tamper protection on servers and endpoints. Adopt behavioural anti-automation controls (rate limiting, sequence-binding) to disrupt script-driven API abuse. Remove internet exposure of internal applications; enforce geofencing under formal change control. Isolate development, testing and production environments. Conduct regular VA/PT including API security testing. Upon detection of suspicious activity: disable compromised accounts, suspend affected APIs, preserve forensic evidence, rotate all credentials, and report to CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin at incident@cert-in.org.in. Reporting Entities are advised to report any signs of suspicious activity related to this attack campaign to CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin at incident@cert-in.org.in , along with all relevant logs, at the earliest.
sources.limitations: Reported Indian financial-sector campaign. Recommendations are not measured effectiveness.

CERT-In reports that attackers used stolen API credentials from victims’ own whitelisted infrastructure to invoke fund-transfer APIs directly, bypass application-level checks and transfer funds to mule accounts.

editorial_building_blocks.2_decision: For one sensitive request, check what proves that this particular action is permitted, beyond a familiar account or company.
editorial_building_blocks.3_concept: Recognizing an account or company is not the same as knowing this particular request is permitted.

4_evidence.purpose: Support and bound the concept, rather than dictate a technical news summary.

beats: Start with the ordinary distinction between having a key and permission to take something.
Explain the two reported incidents in ordinary workplace language; define any indispensable specialist term immediately.
Show why recognizing the account or company does not settle whether this action is permitted.
Give the fixed practical inspection task and retain the limits without a technical lecture.

symbol.image: A working office key establishes that a lock can be opened; it does not establish permission to remove the equipment inside.

mapping.real_relationship: Cloudflare’s stolen credentials remained usable after being left unrotated.
Attackers subsequently accessed Cloudflare’s Atlassian environment.
Conceptual counterpart to authorization for a specific business action; CERT-In reports payment requests bypassing application checks.

symbol.boundary: Digital credentials can be copied and used remotely. A physical key does not represent shared network origins or transaction-stage validation. Removing equipment is illustrative, not an allegation about Cloudflare.

5_telling_voice.voice: relatable_provocateur v1; Graham Hill individual author
5_telling_voice.instruction: Explain ordinary decisions. Translate credentials as account access, whitelisted infrastructure as recognized company systems, API calls as direct computer-to-computer requests only if indispensable. No invented work experience, dialogue, screen-location assumptions or measured outcomes.

questions: Can a non-specialist paraphrase the point?
Is the telling useful beyond its opening?
